title: Latin America’s Second Pink Tide Recedes
gist: Latin America’s second leftward wave ends with Colombia’s handover to right-wing Abelardo de la Espriella, having delivered far less than the first pink tide because it lacked a commodities boom to finance it; the durable legacy is cross-border integration infrastructure (Mercosur’s EU deal, the Capricorn Bioceanic Corridor, a five-country single aviation market) that is surviving the ideological swing.

themes.theme: Commodity Cycle Drives the Ideological Cycle

insights.claim: Latin America’s first pink tide could fund rising social spending, falling inequality, and expanded higher education because a global commodities boom lifted public revenue across the region; the second pink tide had no such tailwind and its anti-poverty programs squeezed government budgets instead.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Treat Latin American fiscal and political durability as a derivative of the commodity cycle — left-led social spending without a terms-of-trade boom converts directly into deficit risk.

insights.claim: The mid-2010s reversal in Latin America was triggered by falling commodity prices, mounting economic problems, and high-profile corruption scandals, which elected a right-wing cohort that then mostly lost power after a single term during COVID-19.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Single-term incumbency punishment is now the regional base case — assume policy reversal risk on roughly four-to-five-year cycles when underwriting long-dated regional exposure.
insights.locator: That momentum gave way in the mid-2010s

insights.claim: By 2023 leftist governments held office in Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, and Peru, but almost all have since exited, leaving Mexico’s Morena and possibly Brazil’s Lula (facing an October vote) as the wave’s only survivors.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Brazil’s October election is the last binary left in the cycle; a Lula loss would complete a region-wide right-wing sweep with implications for Mercosur policy and commodity export regimes.
insights.locator: Latin America’s second pink tide has proved

insights.claim: Colombia’s multidimensional poverty fell to a historic low under Gustavo Petro and Brazil significantly reduced food insecurity, showing the second pink tide did move social indicators even as its flagship political projects failed.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Separate social-outcome performance from market-relevant policy delivery — the two diverged sharply in this cycle.
insights.locator: Several of these governments expanded anti-poverty efforts

insights.claim: The most visible second-pink-tide leaders failed on their signature pledges: Petro’s plan to reduce violence by negotiating with armed groups instead of militarized force, and Gabriel Boric’s proposal to rewrite Chile’s dictatorship-era constitution.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Flagship constitutional and security overhauls in the region have a poor completion record — discount them heavily when pricing announced reform agendas.

insights.claim: Mercosur expanded in 2024 to admit Bolivia and signed its long-delayed deal with the European Union this year, though holding the bloc together required careful diplomacy after Argentine President Javier Milei threatened to withdraw.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: The EU-Mercosur deal is now signed despite the region’s political churn — a concrete trade-flow catalyst for South American agri and EU industrial exporters.
insights.locator: In foreign-policy terms, regional integration survived

insights.claim: Second-pink-tide governments, especially Brazil, revived cross-border infrastructure corridors under discussion since the early 2000s, notably the Capricorn Bioceanic Corridor linking ports on South America’s east and west coasts.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: A functioning bioceanic corridor would reroute South American export logistics toward Pacific shipping — watch port, rail, and freight operators on both coasts.
insights.locator: The leaders of the second pink tide

insights.claim: Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, and Paraguay — two of them now under far-right leaders — signed an agreement last month to create a single aviation market modeled on the EU’s, letting airlines based in one member country operate in the others.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Regional integration is proving ideology-agnostic; South American carriers face a liberalized cross-border operating regime regardless of who wins upcoming elections.

insights.claim: Outside powers, especially the United States and China, pursue agendas in South America focused on accessing commodities with local development left as an afterthought, according to Pedro Silva Barros, former economic affairs director of the Union of South American Nations.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Expect rising host-country friction over extractive-only investment terms; local-content and industrialization conditions are becoming the price of resource access.
insights.quote: “The corridor is more important for connecting these countries to each other than it is for connecting them with China or another extra-regional power,”
insights.locator: Those agendas often focus on accessing the region’s commodities

insights.claim: More than six months after the United States removed Nicolás Maduro and took responsibility for reviving Venezuela’s oil sector, a Financial Times calculation found Washington has collected more than $13 billion in Venezuelan oil revenue this year, while a Venezuelan transparency site has disclosed only a single $300 million transfer.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Opaque handling of $13 billion in oil receipts is a live political-risk headline for any company or creditor with Venezuelan exposure.

insights.claim: The United States had transferred at least $3 billion to Venezuela by April according to a State Department official, but the Trump administration has yet to publish the reports it promised on how the oil revenue is being spent.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: The disclosure gap between $13 billion collected and $3 billion transferred is the metric to track for congressional or legal challenge risk.

insights.claim: Despite Trump administration hopes that U.S. oil companies would move into Venezuela, the largest ones have so far held back from major new investments.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Majors are pricing sovereign and reversal risk above the resource prize — do not assume a Venezuelan capex cycle is imminent even under U.S. administration of the sector.

insights.claim: Bolivia reached a preliminary deal with the IMF for a $1.9 billion loan, with the Fund praising the country’s June decision to move toward a more market-determined exchange rate.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: IMF endorsement plus FX liberalization marks Bolivia as the region’s live macro-adjustment story — relevant to distressed sovereign debt and lithium-sector investors.

insights.claim: President Rodrigo Paz’s first months in office were marked by opposition road blockades across major cities in May and June in which 22 people died, according to Bolivia’s ombudsman’s office, though tensions now appear to have eased.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Social resistance to Bolivian adjustment is violent but so far survivable — renewed blockades are the signal that the IMF program is at risk.
insights.locator: The IMF endorsement is a step forward

insights.claim: Hundreds of thousands of Haitians in the United States lost temporary protected status, and a Haitian migration official said Washington told the government to expect about 250 deportees per week — a pace that could eventually approach the more than 25,000 Venezuelans deported during Trump’s second term.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Large forced-return flows into a collapsed state raise remittance, labor-supply, and regional instability risks worth tracking.
insights.locator: In Focus: U.S. Deportations to Haiti

insights.claim: Gangs still control around 85 percent of the Port-au-Prince metropolitan area and only 1,000 of the up to 5,500 troops authorized by the U.N. Security Council in September 2025 have arrived nearly a year later.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: The international security mission is failing on delivery; Haiti remains a no-go jurisdiction and a source of sustained migration pressure on the Caribbean and the U.S.

insights.claim: The U.S. State Department renewed its “do not travel” advisory for Haiti, advising citizens who travel there to leave copies of their dental records with family in case their remains need identification.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: An official advisory phrased in those terms is the clearest available proxy for total security breakdown — insurers and operators should treat Haiti as uninsurable.

insights.claim: Salvadoran journalists Óscar Martínez and Carlos Martínez won the Gabo prize for an essay on fleeing before Nayib Bukele’s government could arrest them, having earlier exposed a secret government deal with a criminal group.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Press exodus from El Salvador signals deepening opacity in a country other regional governments are now copying on security policy.
insights.quote: “Preventive departures,” they write, “were always a sugar-coated euphemism for exile.”
